name: Word Problems, Warm Ups, and Retake Forms
title: Word Problems, Warm Ups, and Retake Forms
answer: AI tools can generate math word problems, warm up review sets, and parallel retake forms, saving teachers time while keeping the math tied to what students care about and what the class actually struggled with. The teacher still chooses the skills, checks every answer, and compares retake versions side by side, because language tools can state wrong answers confidently and small number changes can shift difficulty.

sections.body: Math teachers need a nearly endless supply of problems, and AI tools can help produce them. Word problems can be built around student interests such as soccer statistics, video game scores, or recipes for a class party, which can make the math feel worth doing. Warm ups can be drawn from the gradebook by looking at skills the class struggled with last month and asking for short review problems on exactly those skills. Retake forms can be generated as parallel versions with different numbers but the same skills and difficulty. The idea solves the time problem of creating varied practice while keeping the teacher in charge of what is taught and what is fair.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a math classroom, the teacher picks the skills and the tool writes the problems. For word problems, the teacher can ask for problems built on student interests like soccer statistics, video game scores, or recipes for a class party. For warm ups, the teacher can look at which skills the class struggled with last month and request short review problems on exactly those skills, spiraling back to old skills a few minutes each day. For retakes, the teacher can ask for a parallel version with different numbers but the same skills and difficulty. The text gives these practices for mathematics across kindergarten through twelfth grade without separating them by grade band.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research, describing what teachers can do with AI tools and what they must check. The only stated basis is the earlier warning from Chapter 1 that language tools can state a wrong answer with complete confidence, which is why the teacher still needs to check every answer.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The teacher still needs to check every answer, since language tools can state a wrong answer with complete confidence. The teacher picks the skills, and the tool writes the problems, so the choice of what to review stays with the person. For retakes, the teacher should compare the two forms carefully, because a small change in numbers can make a problem much easier or harder. A quick side by side check keeps retakes fair. These limits and decisions stay with the teacher rather than the tool.
